newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Central African Republic on ethnic knife edge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Central African Republic on ethnic knife edge.

text.p: In a corner of La Kouanga, a volatile neighbourhood in Central African Republic's capital Bangui, a small boy with a stick crouches and unleashes a furious burst of gunfire on an imaginary AK-47.
For him, at least, it's a game -- still a world away from a Liberia with its rival factions and tragically brutal small boys' brigades, where the word of a teenager with a gun has so often been law.
"It hasn't reached that stage yet," Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, head of an African mediating team, says in between a flurry of meetings.

But with the army divided along ethnic lines and minority Yakomas loyal to former military leader Andre Kolingba in revolt for the third time in under a year, many fear another African nightmare -- Rwanda-style massacres.
The former French colony's influential Roman Catholic bishops have diagnosed tribal hatred as the main threat.
"Tribal violence has touched us in the neighbourhoods where people live with a rare cruelty," Monsignor Paulin Pomodimo, bishop of Bossangoa, told worshippers in Bangui on Sunday.
Ethnic killings have already sparked an exodus of civilians from parts of the capital.
The mutinies began last April over pay but resurfaced in May as part of a wider campaign to oust President Ange-Felix Patasse, a civilian elected in 1993.
The crisis, which has already killed hundreds of people, flared anew on November 15 when Yakomas in the army mutinied again. A fragile truce runs out on January 23.
FRANCE PROTECTS PRESIDENT AND FOREIGNERS
Former colonial power France, its troops in the country under a defence pact, intervened in May, effectively keeping Patasse in power.

French military spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier says France's mission is to restore confidence among the civilian population and protect the symbols of state authority and around 3,000 foreign nationals, two-thirds of them French.
"We have always had a lingering concern for the safety of foreign residents, a fear of reprisals," he says.

But France's presence on the ground, as a buffer between mutineers and the populous southern districts loyal to them and their bitter rivals in the presidential guard, who control the centre and north of the city, has created mixed feelings.

Its reprisals against the mutineers on January 5 after the killing of two French officers on a mediation mission changed the military balance, driving mutineers from most of their strongholds, but they increased hostility among the population.
Most people welcome the return of a semblance of normality, but many, particularly the young, want French troops to leave.
"This is no longer a French colony," one student commented.

"No to France," a virulently anti-French placard says on a makeshift barricade and checkpoint blocking entry to the eastern district of Ouango, a prosperous residential suburb, where mutineers have melted into the local population.
Controlled ostensibly by civilians, the checkpoint restricts access to the French ambassador's residence at night -- with women and youngsters keeping nocturnal vigils.
"We, the civilians, are against the presence of French troops and we all want Patasse to resign," said the student.

The bishops have thrown their weight behind Toumani Toure and his mediating team, mandated by the presidents of Mali, Burkina Faso, Gabon and Chad who visited Bangui at the behest of a Franco-African summit in December.
"The institution of dialogue exists...it must run its course to save the nation from an unnecessary bloodbath. There has been too much blood, too much suffering," Pomodimo said.
FRANCE LOOKS FOR AN EXIT
The bishops trace the conflict back to a social malaise rooted in the impoverished nation's political and economic crisis -- unpaid salaries, strikes, general social discontent.
Toumane Toure, widely respected for the way he stepped down and ushered in democracy in Mali, says the military problem cannot be solved in isolation from the political crisis.

The mutineers, who are showing renewed confidence, want the right to regroup their scattered forces and have a full say in any settlement. "There must be a lasting solution, a radical change," their spokesman Lieutenant Parfait MBay says.
France, caught in the middle, is looking for a dignified way out -- some sources favour the idea of a force of African peacekeepers to go with the African mediation effort.

French diplomats have stepped back, leaving the negotiating to Toumani Toure and his team. Meetings between mediators and mutineers have switched from the French ambassador's residence to the archbishop of Bangui's residence.
On the ground, France has dismantled a major checkpoint at the southwest edge of La Kouanga and is encouraging deployment of Central African police and gendarmes.
Toumani Toure says Central Africans must agree among themselves. His team wants a multi-party conciliation commission to produce a blueprint for peace by Wednesday.

Activists at the barricade in Ouango favour early presidential elections -- Patasse's term does not end until 1999. "He mustn't be allowed to finish his term," the student, 23, commented to nods of approval from those around him.
But in the meantime, a lingering concern, is the widespread distribution of weapons -- both among mutineers and their supporters or militias loyal to Patasse in northern Bangui.
"It's a major problem, there are weapons everywhere," Pelissier says.
